title: Top-K and Kth-Element Patterns
summary: A fixed-size-K heap answers "what are the top K?" in O(n log k), beating a full sort whenever K is small relative to n.

slides.markdown:
"Find the Kth largest", "top K frequent words", "K closest points to the origin" — this whole family shares one shape: you need the best K items out of n, and K is usually much smaller than n.

The heap pattern: keep a heap of exactly **size K**, and for every new candidate, compare it against the heap's current worst-of-the-best. If the new one is better, evict the worst and insert the new one. That caps the heap at size K forever, giving **O(n log k)** total — strictly better than sorting everything at O(n log n) whenever k is small.

The trick that surprises people first: to find the K **largest**, you keep a **min**-heap (not a max-heap) of size K.

To find the **Kth largest** element in a stream, maintain a **min-heap capped at size K**. For each incoming value: push it, and if the heap now has more than K elements, pop the minimum.

After processing everything, the heap holds exactly the K largest values seen so far, and the **root is the Kth largest** — because it's the smallest of that top-K set. This inverts the intuition of "largest → max-heap": you use a min-heap specifically so its root, the thing you can see in O(1), is the boundary value you actually care about (the worst of the best K).

Every element does at most one push and possibly one pop, each O(log k), so the total cost is **O(n log k)** rather than O(n log n) for sorting the whole stream.

```python
import heapq

def kth_largest(stream, k):
    heap = []
    for x in stream:
        heapq.heappush(heap, x)
        if len(heap) > k:
            heapq.heappop(heap)      # evict the current smallest of the top-k
    return heap[0]                   # root = kth largest overall
```

This pattern generalizes directly to a **running** Kth largest over a live stream: keep the same heap object across calls, and `heap[0]` is always the current answer after each new element — no need to re-scan anything that's already been processed.

A related but distinct problem: given a collection, find the **K most frequent** elements, not the K largest values.

The pattern is two phases: **count first, then heap on frequency**. Build a frequency map in one O(n) pass (a hash map counting occurrences), then run the same size-K min-heap pattern from before — but ordered by *count*, not by the element's own value, evicting the lowest-frequency entry whenever the heap exceeds size K.

The heap phase costs O(m log k), where m is the number of **distinct** elements (map size), not the original n — counting has already collapsed duplicates before the heap ever sees them.

```python
import heapq
from collections import Counter

def top_k_frequent(nums, k):
    counts = Counter(nums)               # O(n): count occurrences
    heap = []
    for value, freq in counts.items():
        heapq.heappush(heap, (freq, value))
        if len(heap) > k:
            heapq.heappop(heap)          # evict the least-frequent of the top-k
    return [value for freq, value in heap]
```

The tuple `(freq, value)` puts frequency first, so the min-heap naturally evicts by frequency; `value` only ever breaks ties between equally frequent elements. This is the same shape as [priority-queues-in-practice](priority-queues-in-practice)'s tuple-ordering trick, applied to a derived key instead of a raw input value.

slides.sectionTitle: Heap vs full sort vs quickselect
slides.markdown:
Three ways to answer a top-K or Kth-element question, with genuinely different bounds:

| Approach | Time | Space | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Size-K heap | O(n log k) | O(k) | best when k ≪ n; naturally handles a live stream |
| Full sort | O(n log n) | O(n) (or O(1) in-place) | simplest to write; wasteful when k is small |
| Quickselect (partition-based) | O(n) average, O(n²) worst | O(1) extra | fastest on average for a one-shot Kth-element query on a static array |

Quickselect wins when you need a **single** Kth-element answer on a **static, in-memory** array and don't mind its rare O(n²) worst case (or use median-of-medians for a guaranteed O(n)). The heap wins when data **streams in over time** and you need the running top-K continuously updated, which quickselect can't do incrementally at all — it has to re-run on the whole array.

The single most common mistake in this pattern: pushing **every** element into an unbounded heap, then popping K times at the end.

That's correct, but it's O(n log n) — you've paid to build a heap over the entire input, throwing away the entire benefit of the size-K bound. The whole point of the pattern is capping the heap at K elements *the entire time it runs*, evicting immediately whenever it grows past K, so the heap operations are always O(log k), never O(log n).

At scale the gap is real: with n = 10,000,000 and k = 10, log k ≈ 3.3 versus log n ≈ 23.3 — roughly a 7x difference in the cost of every single heap operation, multiplied across ten million elements.

"K closest points to the origin" (or K nearest neighbors by any distance metric) is the identical pattern with a different **key**: instead of ordering by raw value or frequency, order by distance, and use a **max-heap** of size K instead of a min-heap.

Why max-heap here, not min-heap: you want to keep the K *closest* points, so the point to evict when the heap overflows is the **farthest** one currently kept — which sits at the root of a max-heap ordered by distance. This is the mirror image of the Kth-largest pattern: there, you wanted the largest values, so you evicted the smallest (min-heap root). Here you want the smallest distances, so you evict the largest (max-heap root). The rule is always: **the heap's root is whatever you're about to evict.**

```python
import heapq

def k_closest(points, k):
    heap = []   # max-heap via negation, ordered by squared distance
    for x, y in points:
        dist = x * x + y * y            # squared distance avoids a sqrt call
        heapq.heappush(heap, (-dist, x, y))
        if len(heap) > k:
            heapq.heappop(heap)          # evicts the current farthest point
    return [(x, y) for _, x, y in heap]
```

Two details worth calling out: **squared distance** avoids an unnecessary square root on every comparison (distances only need to be *ordered*, not measured exactly), and the negation trick turns Python's min-heap into the max-heap-by-distance this pattern needs — the same trick from [priority-queues-in-practice](priority-queues-in-practice).

A second common bug: getting the **push/pop order** backwards, or forgetting one of the two entirely.

The pattern must be **push the new candidate first, then check size and pop if needed** — never the reverse. Popping before pushing can evict a value that should have stayed, if the heap was already exactly at size K and the new candidate turns out to be worse than everything currently kept; you'd be discarding a valid member to make room for a candidate that doesn't even deserve to enter.

A quieter version of the same bug: forgetting the pop entirely and just checking `if len(heap) > k` without ever popping — the heap silently grows unbounded, and every subsequent operation costs O(log n) instead of O(log k), with no error to signal it. Always pair every push with a size check, and every size check with an actual pop.

slides.sectionTitle: When the pattern doesn't pay off
slides.markdown:
The size-K heap wins hardest when **k ≪ n**, but the crossover matters: if k is a large fraction of n (say k = n/2), O(n log k) is barely different from O(n log n), and the simpler full-sort approach is often faster in practice — no per-element heap bookkeeping, and modern sort implementations are extremely well-optimized (see [comparing-classic-sorts](comparing-classic-sorts)).

A rule of thumb worth stating out loud in an interview: reach for the size-K heap when k is a small, roughly constant fraction of n or an explicit small constant (top 10, top 100); reach for a full sort when k approaches n or when you need the *entire* ordering anyway, not just the boundary.
